title: Commonly Confused Words
shortDescription: Look-alike, sound-alike word pairs that examiners love — each one taught with the distinction, not just two definitions side by side.
genZNote: These words are basically grammar's identical twins. Learn the one tiny difference and you'll never mix them up again.

sections.heading: affect vs effect
bullets: 'Affect' is (almost always) a VERB meaning 'to influence': 'The weather AFFECTED the match.'
'Effect' is (almost always) a NOUN meaning 'a result': 'The medicine had a positive EFFECT.'
Memory hook: Affect = Action (verb); Effect = End result (noun).
Trap: 'effect' can rarely be a verb meaning 'to bring about' ('to effect a change'), but this is uncommon and usually not the tested case.

sections.heading: stationary vs stationery
bullets: 'Stationary' (with an A) is an ADJECTIVE meaning 'not moving': 'The car remained stationary.'
'Stationery' (with an E) is a NOUN meaning writing materials (paper, pens): 'She bought stationery for the office.'
Memory hook: stationEry has an E, like Envelope/pEn.

sections.heading: principal vs principle
bullets: 'Principal' can be a NOUN (the head of a school) or an ADJECTIVE (main/most important): 'The PRINCIPAL reason', 'the college PRINCIPAL.'
'Principle' is always a NOUN meaning a fundamental rule or belief: 'He acted on PRINCIPLE.'
Memory hook: princiPAL is your PAL (a person); principLE is a ruLE.

sections.heading: complement vs compliment
bullets: 'Complement' means something that completes or goes well with something else: 'The scarf COMPLEMENTS her dress.'
'Compliment' means a polite expression of praise: 'He paid her a COMPLIMENT.'
Memory hook: complIment = I like to give praise; complEment completEs.

sections.heading: More frequently confused pairs
bullets: Lose (verb, to misplace/fail to win) vs Loose (adjective, not tight): 'Don't LOSE the LOOSE change.'
Its (possessive, 'belonging to it') vs It's (contraction of 'it is'): 'IT'S raining, so the dog is in ITS kennel.'
Than (used in comparisons) vs Then (referring to time/sequence): 'She is taller THAN him; THEN we left.'
Council (a group that governs/advises) vs Counsel (advice, or to advise): 'The town COUNCIL sought legal COUNSEL.'
Born (to be brought into life) vs Borne (past participle of 'bear', to carry/endure): 'She was BORN in 1990'; 'the cost was BORNE by the company.'
Elicit (to draw out a response) vs Illicit (illegal): 'The lawyer tried to ELICIT the truth about the ILLICIT deal.'
Adapt (to adjust) vs Adopt (to take on/take in): 'He ADAPTED to the new city and ADOPTED a stray dog.'

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Commonly confused words look or sound similar but differ in meaning or part of speech — each pair is best learned through a distinguishing memory hook, not a plain definition.
keyFacts: Affect = verb (to influence); Effect = noun (a result).
Principal = head/main; Principle = a rule or belief.
commonConfusion: Nearly every pair on this page is, itself, the 'common confusion' — that is the entire point of the topic.

highYieldFacts: Affect/effect and its/it's are two of the single most frequently tested confusable pairs in all competitive English sections.
commonTraps: Using 'effect' where a verb is needed, or 'affect' where a noun is needed.
Writing 'stationary' when referring to paper and pens (should be 'stationery').
mustRemember: Use the memory hooks (stationEry/Envelope, princiPAL/PAL) to recall spelling under exam pressure.

confusedTerms.distinction: 'Affect' is a verb meaning to influence something. 'Effect' is a noun meaning the result of that influence.
'Its' shows possession ('the dog wagged its tail'). "It's" is a contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'.

possibleQuestions: Choose the correct word: 'The heavy rain badly ___ (effected/affected) the crop yield.'
Choose the correct word: 'Please buy some ___ (stationary/stationery) from the shop.'
